note.title: Non-communicable diseases, lifestyle factors and cancer
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Non-communicable diseases come from inherited factors and lifestyle, often several together
Obesity: energy used lower than energy intake; it leads to cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes
Tar: bronchitis (narrowed bronchi and bronchioles), emphysema (damaged alveoli, less surface area), lung cancer
Nicotine: addictive, affects the heart rate. Carbon monoxide: combines with red blood cells, less oxygen carried
Alcohol: binge drinking damages the liver; in pregnancy, foetal alcohol syndrome
Cancer: uncontrolled cell division. Benign: encapsulated, does not spread. Malignant: can spread
Lower the risk: HPV vaccine (cervical), not smoking (lung), avoiding UV (skin)

noteBlocks.lede: Some diseases cannot be caught at all. They come from the genes you inherit and the way you live: what you eat, how much you move, alcohol, tobacco and the Sun. This topic links each cause to its harm, and shows how cancer starts and spreads.
can: Sort the causes of a non-communicable disease, and explain how obesity leads to other diseases.
Link tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide to their effects, and describe what alcohol does.
Describe cancer as uncontrolled cell division, tell benign from malignant, and lower the risk of three cancers.

noteBlocks.md: A cold passes from person to person. Lung cancer, heart disease and Type 2 diabetes never do, yet between them they cause far more deaths. They come from inside: from the genes people inherit and from the way they live, and a few choices change the odds a great deal.

noteBlocks.caption: Six things that can add up to a non-communicable disease. Often several act together.

noteBlocks.md: A **non-communicable disease** is not caused by a pathogen, so nobody can catch it. It comes from two kinds of cause. Some are **inherited**: a person may carry a gene that makes some cancers more likely. Others are **lifestyle**: a poor diet with too much sugar and fat, too little exercise, too much Sun, and misusing alcohol or tobacco. Most of these diseases come from several causes acting together.

Lung cancer is non-communicable: no pathogen causes it, and it cannot pass from one person to another. Tuberculosis is not, although it also harms the lungs: a bacterium causes it, and it spreads in droplets from coughs.

noteBlocks.stem: Conor's father and grandfather both had bowel cancer, and Conor smokes. Give one inherited factor and one lifestyle factor that raise his risk of cancer, and say why his friends cannot catch cancer from him.

steps.working: Inherited: he may carry a gene, passed down his family, that makes some cancers more likely.
steps.decision: Two relatives with the same cancer point to a gene. A gene raises the risk; it does not make cancer certain.

steps.working: Lifestyle: smoking, because the tar in the smoke can cause lung cancer.
steps.decision: A lifestyle factor is something he does, and he can change it.

steps.working: Cancer is non-communicable: no pathogen causes it, so there is nothing to pass on.
steps.decision: Ask whether there is a pathogen. Without one, a disease cannot be caught.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is a lifestyle factor, not an inherited one, that raises the risk of a non-communicable disease?
options: binge drinking
a gene that raises the risk of some cancers
catching flu from a classmate
noteBlocks.explain: Sort each option as See it sorted Conor's risks: a lifestyle factor is something a person does, and binge drinking harms the liver. A gene is inherited, and flu is caught from a virus, so it is communicable. The answer is binge drinking.

twin.prompt: Aoife's mother and grandmother both had heart disease. Aoife eats a lot of sugary, fatty food, and last month she caught tuberculosis. Which of these is a lifestyle factor in her risk of a non-communicable disease?
options: her diet high in sugar and fat
her family history of heart disease
the tuberculosis she caught
twin.answer: her diet high in sugar and fat
twin.explain: A lifestyle factor is something she does, and she can change her diet. A family history points to inherited genes, and tuberculosis is caught from a bacterium, so it is communicable. The answer is her diet high in sugar and fat.

optionNotes.option: her family history of heart disease
optionNotes.why: Two relatives with the same disease point to a gene she may have inherited, which is not a way of living she chose.

optionNotes.option: the tuberculosis she caught
optionNotes.why: Tuberculosis is caught from a bacterium, so it is a communicable disease, not a lifestyle factor in one that cannot be caught.

optionNotes.option: a gene that raises the risk of some cancers
optionNotes.why: Genes do raise the risk, which makes it tempting, but a gene is inherited, not a way of living you choose.

optionNotes.option: catching flu from a classmate
optionNotes.why: It is a real illness, but flu is caught from a virus, so it is a communicable disease, not a cause of one that cannot be caught.

noteBlocks.md: Food gives the body energy, and exercise uses it. When the **energy used in exercise is lower than the energy taken in**, the extra is **stored as fat**, and over months a person can become **obese**. A diet with too much sugar and fat makes this more likely.

noteBlocks.caption: One disease can lead to others: obesity raises the risk of two more.

noteBlocks.md: Non-communicable diseases can lead to one another. Obesity raises the risk of **cardiovascular disease**, disease of the heart and blood vessels, and of **Type 2 diabetes**, in which the body can no longer control its blood glucose properly.

noteBlocks.stem: Each day Niamh takes in 10,400 kJ of energy from food and uses 9,100 kJ. Explain what will happen to her body mass if this goes on for months.

steps.working: 10,400 − 9,100 = 1,300 kJ more taken in than used each day.
steps.decision: Compare energy in with energy used first; the difference decides everything.

steps.working: The extra energy is stored in her body as fat, so her mass rises.
steps.decision: Say where the extra energy goes. Stored as fat is the phrase the scheme wants.

steps.working: Over months she could become obese, which raises her risk of cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes.
steps.decision: End on the consequence: one non-communicable disease leading to others.

noteBlocks.prompt: Each day Ryan takes in 9,800 kJ from food and uses 10,300 kJ. What happens to his stored fat if this goes on?
options: it is used up, so his mass falls
it builds up, so his mass rises
it stays the same
noteBlocks.answer: it is used up, so his mass falls
noteBlocks.explain: Compare in with used, as See it did: he uses 500 kJ more than he takes in each day, so the body makes up the difference from its stored fat. Fat builds up only when more comes in than is used. The answer is that it is used up, so his mass falls.

twin.prompt: Each day Siobhan takes in 8,600 kJ from food and uses 8,600 kJ. What happens to her stored fat if this goes on?
options: it stays the same
it builds up, so her mass rises
it is used up, so her mass falls
twin.explain: Compare energy in with energy used: 8,600 kJ each, so there is no extra energy to store and none missing to make up from fat. The answer is that it stays the same.

optionNotes.option: it builds up, so her mass rises
optionNotes.why: Fat builds up only when more energy comes in than is used, and here the two are equal.

optionNotes.option: it is used up, so her mass falls
optionNotes.why: Stored fat is used only when more energy is used than comes in, and here the two match.

optionNotes.option: it builds up, so his mass rises
optionNotes.why: That is what happens when more energy comes in than is used, and here it is the other way round.

optionNotes.option: it stays the same
optionNotes.why: It would stay the same only if energy in matched energy used exactly, and here he uses more than he eats.

noteBlocks.caption: Alcohol in one person's blood after an evening's drinking. The liver removes it slowly and steadily.

noteBlocks.md: **Binge drinking** is drinking a lot of alcohol in a short time. Over the years, heavy drinking causes **liver disease**, because the liver is the organ that breaks alcohol down. Alcohol also affects judgement and behaviour. In pregnancy, alcohol reaches the foetus through the placenta and can cause **foetal alcohol syndrome**, which harms the baby's development. The guideline is no more than 14 units a week, spread over several days.

On a blood-alcohol graph, a steep rise to a high peak shows a lot drunk in a short time. To find how long the level stayed over a line, read where the curve crosses it going up and coming down, then subtract.

noteBlocks.stem: The graph in the figure shows the alcohol in Seán's blood after an evening out. How does it show binge drinking, and for how long was he over the legal driving limit?

steps.working: It rises steeply to 160 mg per 100 cm³ within 1 hour.
steps.decision: A lot of alcohol in a short time is binge drinking: quote the peak and how quickly it came.

steps.working: It crosses the limit of 80 at 0.5 hours going up and at 5 hours coming down.
steps.decision: Read both crossings straight down to the time axis; say what you read before you use it.

steps.working: 5 − 0.5 = 4.5 hours over the limit.
steps.decision: Subtract the earlier time from the later one: the time it came down is not the answer on its own.

noteBlocks.prompt: On another person's graph, the blood alcohol level rises above the driving limit at 1 hour and falls back below it at 7.5 hours. For how many hours was it above the limit? Give the number only.
noteBlocks.explain: Subtract the time it went above the limit from the time it came back below, as step 3 of See it did: 7.5 − 1 = 6.5. The time it came down, 7.5, is when it ended, not how long it lasted. The answer is 6.5.

twin.prompt: A third graph crosses the limit at 1.5 hours going up and at 7 hours coming down. For how many hours was the level above the limit? Give the number only.
twin.explain: Later crossing minus earlier crossing: 7 − 1.5 = 5.5. The answer is 5.5.

noteBlocks.md: **Tar** harms the lungs three ways. In **bronchitis** the bronchi and bronchioles become narrower. In **emphysema** the walls of the alveoli are damaged, so there is less surface for gas exchange. In **lung cancer**, cells in the lungs begin abnormal, uncontrolled division. **Nicotine** is **addictive**, which is why smokers find it hard to stop, and it changes the **heart rate**. **Carbon monoxide** joins onto red blood cells, so the blood can carry less oxygen.

noteBlocks.title: Why emphysema leaves a person breathless
noteBlocks.md: Many small alveoli give a huge surface for oxygen to diffuse into the blood. When their walls break down into a few large sacs, the surface shrinks, so less oxygen reaches the blood for respiration, and even a short walk leaves the person out of breath.

noteBlocks.title: Link each effect to its chemical
noteBlocks.md: In the Summer 2025 six-mark question on smoking, each mark was for an effect linked to the right chemical, and the report found tar and nicotine mixed up. Write the chemical and its effect in the same sentence.

noteBlocks.stem: A smoker has three problems: narrowed airways and a cough, a resting heart rate that is too high, and blood that carries less oxygen than it should. Name the chemical in tobacco smoke behind each one, and say what it does.

steps.working: Narrowed airways: tar, which narrows the bronchi and bronchioles (bronchitis).
steps.decision: Airways and lungs always point to tar.

steps.working: The high heart rate: nicotine, which affects the heart rate.
steps.decision: Anything about the heart rate belongs to nicotine.

steps.working: Less oxygen: carbon monoxide, which combines with red blood cells.
steps.decision: Anything about the blood carrying oxygen is carbon monoxide.

noteBlocks.md: Cells divide by mitosis for growth and repair, and the division stops when enough cells are made. **Cancer** cells come from **uncontrolled cell division**: they keep dividing and form a lump called a **tumour**. Drawn beside normal cells, cancer cells are usually **larger**, with **larger nuclei** and **thicker membranes**, and are **irregular** in shape and arrangement.

noteBlocks.md: A **benign** tumour is **encapsulated**, held inside a capsule, and does **not spread**, so it can often be removed. A **malignant** tumour has no capsule and is **capable of spreading**: its cells can break away and travel in the blood to other parts of the body, where they form new tumours.

noteBlocks.title: Reading a tumour from a drawing
noteBlocks.md: Say only what the drawing shows: larger cells, larger nuclei, thicker membranes, irregular. No capsule, and cells inside a blood vessel, mean malignant. In Summer 2024 many lost marks by not using the drawing.

noteBlocks.stem: Give three differences, shown in the figure, between the cancer cells and the normal cells.

steps.working: The cancer cells are larger than the normal cells.
steps.decision: Compare the same feature on both sides, and name which cells you mean.

steps.working: The cancer cells have larger nuclei.
steps.decision: The nucleus is a separate feature from the whole cell, so it is a second difference.

steps.working: The cancer cells have thicker membranes (outlines).
steps.decision: Only what is drawn counts: the outlines are drawn thicker.

steps.working: The cancer cells are irregular in shape and jumbled, not in neat rows.
steps.decision: A fourth difference in case one is doubted: the arrangement.

noteBlocks.answer: their nuclei are larger than those of the normal cells
noteBlocks.explain: Evidence is something you can point at in the drawing, as every step of See it did. Uncontrolled division is true but not drawn, and UV is a guess. The answer is that their nuclei are larger than those of the normal cells.

optionNotes.option: benign tumours are less dangerous

optionNotes.option: cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division
optionNotes.why: It is true, but it is a fact you knew before you looked, not something the drawing shows.

optionNotes.option: the cells may have been damaged by UV light
optionNotes.why: It may be possible, but nothing in the drawing shows UV, so it is a guess, not evidence.

noteBlocks.caption: Three cancers, and a choice that lowers the risk of each.

noteBlocks.md: Some choices lower the risk of particular cancers. **Cervical cancer** is linked to **HPV**, a virus passed on during sex: the **HPV vaccine**, offered in the first years of secondary school, and condoms lower the risk. **Lung cancer** is linked to the tar in tobacco smoke: not smoking lowers the risk.

**Skin cancer** is linked to **ultraviolet (UV) radiation** from the Sun and sunbeds, which causes **mutations** in skin cells that can lead to uncontrolled cell division: sunscreen, shade, covering up and a hat, and avoiding sunbeds, lower the risk.

noteBlocks.stem: Maya has the HPV vaccine at 12, Tom stops smoking, and Grace stops using a sunbed. Explain how each change lowers a cancer risk.

steps.working: Maya: the vaccine protects her against HPV, the virus that can lead to cervical cancer.
steps.decision: Name the cancer, then the link: the vaccine works on the virus.

steps.working: Tom: tar no longer reaches his lungs, so there is less risk of the abnormal cell division that starts lung cancer.
steps.decision: Name the chemical that does the harm.

steps.working: Grace: a sunbed gives out UV radiation, which causes mutations in skin cells, so without it her risk of skin cancer falls.
steps.decision: Say UV, never just 'the sun': the precise word is what earns the mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which choice lowers the risk of lung cancer, and why?

having the HPV vaccine, so tar cannot cause cancer
noteBlocks.answer: not smoking, so tar no longer reaches the lungs
noteBlocks.explain: Match each choice to its cancer, as See it matched Tom's: lung cancer is linked to the tar in tobacco smoke. Sunscreen works against UV and skin cancer, and the vaccine against HPV and cervical cancer. The answer is not smoking, so tar no longer reaches the lungs.

noteBlocks.md: **A number that is already a percentage.** A paper may give the number of people with one cancer and the percentage of all cancers it makes, and ask for the total. Divide by the percentage to find 1%, then multiply by 100. The total must come out larger than the part. (Summer 2019 Foundation.)
**The precise word.** Cancer cells come from uncontrolled (or abnormal) cell division, not just cell division; skin cancer is caused by UV radiation, not just the Sun. (Summer 2024 report.)

noteBlocks.stem: In one year, 2,610 people in a region were diagnosed with bowel cancer. This was 18% of all the cancers diagnosed there that year. Calculate the total number of cancers diagnosed.

steps.decision: 2,610 is already the 18%, so divide by 18 to find 1%.
Check: the total, 14,500, is larger than the part, 2,610, as a whole must be.

noteBlocks.prompt: 3,150 people is 21% of all the people treated at a clinic in one year. How many people were treated there in total? Give the number only.
noteBlocks.explain: The 3,150 is already the 21%, so find 1% first, as See it did: 3,150 ÷ 21 = 150, then × 100 = 15,000. Working out 21% of 3,150 gives a smaller number, which a total cannot be. The answer is 15,000.

Say what makes a disease non-communicable, and sort its causes into inherited and lifestyle.
Explain obesity as more energy in than used, and link it to cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes.
Give the harm done by alcohol, and read time over a limit from a graph.
Link tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide each to its own effects.
Describe cancer, tell benign from malignant, and lower the risk of three cancers.

This topic comes every year: short recall (the chemical, the tumour type, UV), data on alcohol or cancer numbers, and some years a six-mark answer on smoking or on a diagram of cancer cells. context.setting: How cancer starts, and the two types of tumour

parts.stem: Cancer cells arise from a process that goes wrong in the body. Name this process.

context.setting: Three people's drinking over one weekend, against a weekly guideline

parts.stem:
The guideline is that no more than 14 units of alcohol should be drunk in one week. One pint of beer contains 2 units and one measure of gin contains 1 unit. The table shows what three people drank over one weekend; none of them drank alcohol from Monday to Thursday.
Calculate the number of units person Q drank over the weekend.
hints: Pints of beer are worth 2 units each; measures of gin 1 unit each. Add up all three days.

parts.stem: Whose drinking over the weekend was the least healthy?

options.feedback: Person P drank 6 units, within the weekly guideline of 14.
Person Q drank 10 units, within the weekly guideline of 14.
Person R: 18 units, more than the guideline of 14 for the whole week, all drunk on one day.

parts.workedSolution: Person R.

parts.stem: Give two reasons for your answer.

accepted: 18 units is more than the guideline of 14 for a week, and it was all drunk in one day, which is binge drinking

scheme.for: the most units / more than the weekly guideline (18 units, over 14)
all drunk in one day: binge drinking

hints: One reason is about how much; the other is about how quickly.
parts.workedSolution: Person R drank 18 units, more than the guideline of 14 for a whole week, and drank all of it on one day, which is binge drinking.

context.setting: Skin cancer as a share of all cancers diagnosed in a region in one year

parts.stem:
In one region in one year, 4,620 people were diagnosed with skin cancer. This was 35% of all the people diagnosed with any type of cancer that year.
Calculate how many people in the region were diagnosed with cancer of any type that year.
hints: 4620 is 35% of the total. Find 1% first, then 100%.
parts.workedSolution: 4620 ÷ 35 = 132 people for each 1%; × 100 = 13,200 people.

commonErrors.feedback: That works out 35% of 4620, a smaller number, but 4620 is already the 35%. The operations go the other way: 4620 ÷ 35 × 100.

context.setting: Two harmful chemicals in tobacco smoke besides carbon monoxide

parts.stem:
Carbon monoxide is one harmful chemical in tobacco smoke. Name two other harmful chemicals in tobacco smoke, and for each one describe how it damages health.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: At least five of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

At least three of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
At least one of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; ideas in an order that is hard to follow; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave what you meant unclear.

indicativeContent.point: tar causes bronchitis: the bronchi and bronchioles become narrower
tar causes emphysema: the alveoli are damaged, reducing the surface area for gas exchange
tar causes lung cancer: abnormal, uncontrolled cell division in the lungs

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] at least five points, Band B [3]-[4] at least three, Band C [1]-[2] at least one, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Each effect earns only when it is linked to the right chemical: bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer belong to tar, addiction and the heart rate to nicotine. An answer that gives tar's effects to nicotine, or the reverse, caps below Band A: the Summer 2025 report found the two mixed up.

hints: Two chemicals, each with its own effects: one damages the airways and lungs, the other acts on the brain and heart.
The words that lift an answer are tar, bronchitis, narrowed, emphysema, alveoli, surface area, lung cancer, nicotine, addictive and heart rate.
parts.workedSolution: Tar is one harmful chemical. It causes bronchitis, in which the bronchi and bronchioles become narrower. It also causes emphysema, which damages the alveoli and reduces the surface area for gas exchange, and it can cause lung cancer, where cells in the lungs begin uncontrolled cell division. Nicotine is the other chemical. Nicotine is addictive, which is why smokers find it hard to stop, and it affects the heart rate.

commonErrors.feedback: Check which chemical does what. Tar damages the airways and lungs (bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer); nicotine is the addictive one, and it affects the heart rate.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dara is asked: 'In one year, 1,020 people in a region died of lung cancer. This was 24% of all deaths from cancer that year. Calculate the total number of deaths from cancer. [2]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 works out 24% of 1020, but 1020 is already the 24%. A total cannot be smaller than one of its parts, so 244.8 is the signal: divide by 24 to find 1%, then multiply by 100.
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 reads the question well, but the method mark is for the right operations: 1020 ÷ 24 × 100 = 4,250. Check: 24% of 4,250 gives back 1020.
